T17 asked a question, and I decided it myself because it's inside the milestone. T17's job is to decide the struct types for the census's leftover "drift" sites. These are cast sites that no struct type covers yet, and fixing them turns the casts into proper member accesses in the C source. Its two rounds brought the undecided cast sites down from 8,146 on 870 types to 6 on 2 types. About 1,640 casts became member accesses, and every batch passed 218 of 218. The md, main and shared segments have no drift left, and all 6 remaining sites are in the overlays.

**What I decided:**
- **One short extra round for the last 6 sites.** It writes 2 struct definitions, sweeps the overlays and re-checks everything. The expert estimates about 30 minutes. If any sites remain after that, they're recorded as a known remainder and T17 closes.
- **One failing done-when check goes to T18.** It comes from 1 unbacked cast and 3 wrong declarations that sit in T18's files, not from T17's work. So T18's fix will count for it, and T17 doesn't touch T18's files. I've logged that in the plan's change list.

**Also of note:**
- **A coder slip, caught and undone.** One coder ran a ledger restamp the brief didn't ask for, then undid it by truncating those 5,680 rows. A copy of them is saved.
- **The struct check passes again.** It had been failing before T17 started, because of earlier tasks, and T17 repaired it.

The install is running now, after which T17 goes on.

PA3 updated from 3.32.8 to 3.32.9. It fixes the bug we just wrote up, and it removes the main things that kept DeepSeek in learning mode.

- **The `../` false refusals are fixed.** The "outside the project" rule now reads a relative path from the folder the coder's shell is actually in, and it follows each `cd` in the command. A quoted string, like a C include path, and a path containing a variable now go to the judge instead of being refused outright. You don't need to file the GitHub issue. If you haven't sent it yet, you can drop it.
- **Learning mode is fairer.** A whole read of a big file that the read guard turned into an outline no longer counts as friction. That was DeepSeek's most common leftover slip. Calls the judge couldn't answer because of a usage limit don't count either.
- **A tidier journal in git.** Git now gets only packed day files instead of thousands of small ones. The update adds a `.gitignore` line for the live folders. A long session also packs the journal every 8 hours.
- **Smaller fixes.** The usage summary switches to the new version right away. 3.32.8's savings repair now finishes even if it's interrupted. The Project line no longer shows an empty `· ·`.

DeepSeek's third note, "never put `../` in a command", is now only a precaution. It's harmless, so I'd leave it.

Project Architect 3.32.9, a hotfix (A tidier journal, and fixes that take effect at once), is installed.

**To load it: /exit, then claude --continue (not /clear)**

The mod's own files changed, so nothing starts until you restart. That includes my queued answer to T17, which goes through after the restart.

Yes, we are. The lever series is current, and the story and retrospective are booked for this phase's close, which is how the last two phases did it too. There's one timing difference from the original rule, which I'd keep.

**What the rule says.** It's your legacy memory from September, with two parts:
- **The lever series.** After every task that changes the lever count, `lever_progress --snapshot` adds a row to `docs/lever-progress.tsv` and updates `docs/levers.md`. Levers are the pins and compiler hints still in the code.
- **The story.** This is the narrative of the work after the game reached 100% matching: story §10 and retrospective §7, plus the timeline chart and the wiki. The memory said to advance it at the end of every session.

**Where it stands now:**
- **The lever series is current.** Its last row, "P40 T11", was written on 2026-11-06 when T11 closed, and T11 was this phase's big lever-cutting task. T17 and T18 didn't change the lever count. T19, running now, only tags the remaining levers by their "wall", the compiler limit that keeps each one in, so the count doesn't move. T13, the milestone gate, takes the phase's closing snapshot.
- **The story is booked.** T14 is the phase-close docs task. It adds Phase 40's part to story §10 and its row to §11, and extends retrospective §7 with its four questions. It also updates the wiki and regenerates the README graphs. On top of that, it carries your 2026-10-15 and 10-17 additions: the "sooner" lessons and the rules for new projects go into the how-to-ai-decomp guide and its wiki pages.

**The one difference.** The story moves once per phase, not once per session. Phases 3.38 and 3.39 worked the same way. Nothing gets lost in between, because each task writes its findings into its summary and log, and T14 builds the story from those.

**My recommendation.** Keep it per phase. In PA3 a session no longer lines up with a unit of work, so a per-session story step would mostly rewrite paragraphs mid-phase. If you want, I can add a line to the card's Developer section that says so, so the old per-session wording doesn't mislead anyone later.

The question about the headless Ghidra is still open. Did you mean for it to run? I've released the talk hold, since this doesn't change the plan.

Phase 3.40 is finished and needs your word to close it. Its milestone gate passed in full at one commit (aace727c4c), from a clean tree, with all 218 game binaries still rebuilding byte-identical.

**What the phase did.** It had two goals. The first was to give the struct types left undecided after 3.39 a single agreed definition, so the casts that use them become member accesses. The second was to make every remaining compiler hint justify itself. A compiler hint here means a pin (forcing a value into a specific register) or a piece of inline asm.
- **Struct types.** Undecided struct types (TNC) went from 291,819 cast sites to 0, across the planned band and the "drift" types that the sweeps created along the way. The leftover tail of rare, mostly one-site types is recorded under its own cause: 5,871 sites, under the frozen cap of 6,976. Tens of thousands of casts became member accesses, and kept casts all have their backing.
- **Declarations.** Function declarations that disagree with their definitions went from 11 to 0. 162 pins became real function parameters.
- **Compiler hints.** 220 functions came free of their hints in the big crack wave, which ran on DeepSeek. 18 shared "head classes" cracked and were copied into every overlay that uses them. Hint sites went from 3,364 to 1,853, and ledger rows from 2,433 to 1,180.
- **The wall rule.** Every surviving hint now names its "wall": the specific gcc pass that plain C can't steer around. The names come from a 35-word vocabulary in `config/lever_walls.tsv`, and `lever_census` fails if any row lacks a wall or uses an unknown one.
- **Record.** Ledger backups are done: a stripped public copy is in `docs/ledgers/`, and the full copy is in your private archive clone. Story §10, retrospective §7, the wiki and the graphs are updated. The waiting cookbook lessons are banked.

**Left open, none of it blocking the close:**
- **Only you can do this.** Push the archive clone, `/home/musashi/BFM-decomp-archive`. It's one commit ahead of origin. Then push this repo as usual.
- **Return-type mismatches aren't counted.** The "0 disagreeing declarations" check doesn't look at return types. For example, func_8016130C still has 1,213 `void` declarations against an `s32` definition. A later phase needs a check for this.
- **A decision for you, low priority.** The public ledger copy dropped the C before/after text from the hint ledger, because a safety scan matched pin notes like `__asm__("$2")`. The archive copy keeps that text. I'd leave it out unless you want the C text public. If you do, it's a small follow-up.
- **Small items for a later tools task:**
  - Three tool bugs found in T21: a crash in `type_census --no-cache`, `struct_twins.py` reading a stale census by default, and `lift_types --fold` leaving an old comment behind.
  - Nine "expand-hardreg-var" wall tags from T20 deserve a second look before any crack wave relies on them.
- **Kept on purpose.** In T9, func_80177B5C (133 rows) only matches with a do-nothing line that steers the compiler. That's a hint written in C, so it wasn't counted as hint-free.

Once you close, I'll start the external-coder review of this phase's 73 DeepSeek runs in the background and bring you its proposals.

The headless Ghidra question is still open too, whenever you have a moment.

- **Lanes and effort stay as they are.** DeepSeek keeps 4 lanes at high effort.

**The two proposed changes:**
1. **Drop DeepSeek note 3**, the "never put `../` in a command" one. I said earlier it was harmless to keep. With the evidence that the fix holds, I now agree it can go.
2. **Remove 36 learned permission rules.** Each one let a coder re-run a helper script it wrote for one T11 shard, for example `.run/P40/T11/RM2/_tools/score.sh`. T11 is closed, so these only leave old self-written scripts pre-approved. The 6 shared helper rules stay.

**Small PA3 quirks, nothing for you to do:**
- The health report doesn't say which file the read guard blocked.
- A judge call with no answer is still counted as friction.
- Some runs show impossibly low turn counts.

## Rationale
- Order: baselines first (T1), so every gate change is measured against a known verdict and runtime. Tool bugs (T2) before the gates, because `--no-cache` and the stale twins default sit under the census T3-T5 rely on. Return-type detector (T3) before its fixes (T4) before the `--check` alignment and wiring (T5), so tools-health turns green once, not red-then-green. The attribution fold (T6) lands in `lever_census --check`, which tools-health already runs. Ghidra types (T7) are independent of the census gates but read the final headers, so they follow T4 (T4 may edit prototypes, not structs; T7 may run in parallel with T5/T6). The live-DB mirror (T8) waits for the R32 answer. The record (T9) and the gate (T10) come last; close docs (T11) after the gate, as in 3.40.
- `--check` semantics: aligning the raw-cast clause to the residue-ledger measure is a change to a gate's meaning, so it is written down as a developer decision with the recommendation, not done silently (house rule: never redefine a term to make a failure pass). The raw count stays printed and in the readability series.
- Return lies in scope: the gate's job is to stop 3.38-3.40 regressing before renames; renames on a lying prototype would carry the lie. If T3 counts more than 300 functions, T4 stops after bucketing them (by return-type pair, caller-use pattern, shared-header fan-out) and Claude brings the buckets to the developer, who picks the stop rule.
- Ghidra type set: the 6 programs with committed files are the rostered set `ghidra_roster.py --check` and the proof already cover; each gets the canonical types its translation units use (census use), and every canonical type lands in at least one proven program (main carries the engine types). Generated type rows are a generated artifact: one tool writes them from the headers, a freshness check fails when the headers moved, and they are never hand-edited (H1). Whether they share the hand-authored `<prog>.jsonl` or sit in a generated sibling the rebuild imports first is the T7 expert's design call, with the proof's byte `cmp` kept exact.
- Layout truth: Ghidra struct offsets must equal gcc's. T7's control compares a sample of exported Ghidra struct field offsets and sizes with gcc's own (audit-cdecl / `offsetof` through the pinned cc1), plus the rebuild's negative control (one mutated field → PROOF FAIL).
- effort: no task is `effort: high`; every done-when is arbitrated by a tool (the gates, the proof, R22).
- Coder tiers: all in-house (card: cracking is DeepSeek-only and nothing here cracks; the rest is gate design, tool edits and doc work).

## Risks
- `--check`'s raw-cast clause: if the developer keeps it, the milestone cannot be green this generation; T5 then returns `blocked` and the milestone needs his amendment.
- Return-lie volume: func_8016130C alone has 1,213 declarations; if lies are widespread and shared-header fan-out is high, T4 grows past the phase (stop rule at 300 functions). Some honest return types may move caller bytes (C0543), leaving ledgered exceptions.
- Attribution vocabulary: 3.39/3.40 markers may not name an instrument at all; fixing marker text across many files is comment-only but still needs R22.
- tools-health wall time: one more fresh census (all of src/ and headers) per run, plus `--strict --residue`; measured at T1. If it exceeds what the low-memory guard tolerates in the foreground, T5 says so and keeps the cheapest form that still gates.
- Ghidra: the proof runs need :8080 free and a Ghidra install at ~/ghidra_12.1_PUBLIC; a foreign headless Ghidra (R32) may hold memory or the port. Header constructs (unions, bitfields, attributes) may not map to row kinds cleanly; ExportAnnotations sorts types by path, so row order must match for the byte `cmp`. Each rebuild is up to 6 headless runs with a 3600 s timeout each.
- T8 waits on the developer (R32 and `/mcp`); if he does not answer, the live-DB part of the milestone waits, while the proof (scratch) can still pass.
- `make clean` wipes `build/ghidra_rebuild/proj`: proof and R22 must never overlap.

You don't need to do anything with Ghidra right now. You're right that it's the Ghidra MCP server, started at session start, so that question is closed. Only the connection to it failed earlier. On the rules: I should have explained them before asking you to approve. Here they are.

**Ghidra.** T1 found the MCP Ghidra serving port 8080. The proof rebuild, which checks that our type text rebuilds Ghidra's database correctly, refuses to run while that port is in use. So T1 will soon come back with a question. When it does, I'll recommend letting the task stop the MCP Ghidra for the length of the proof, about 6 rebuilds. After that you run `/mcp` once to reconnect. Don't turn it off or reconnect it yourself before then.

**Rule T2, finishing the ledger after each batch.** A "decision batch" is a set of struct-type decisions applied to the source: define a type, merge it into another, or leave it as residue. Each kept cast needs a ledger row giving its reason. After a batch, three bookkeeping commands keep the ledger honest. `--residue` writes rows for casts that are left, `--restamp` updates the reason recorded on each row, and `--check-residue` confirms every cast is covered. The rule says a batch isn't done until all three have run on every segment it touched.
- **For:** skipping them in 3.40 cost real time. There were 3,457 stale reasons on one type, and 124 rewritten functions had no rows at all. Both were found tasks later and had to be reconstructed.
- **Against:** it adds a few minutes per batch, even when nothing changed.

**Rule T3, marking generated code inside hand-edited headers.** Some headers, like `include/struct_types.h`, are partly written by tools and partly by hand. The rule says a tool-written block gets a start and an end comment, plus one line naming the tool and the commit it ran at.
- **For:** anyone can see which lines not to hand-edit, and a tool can regenerate its block without touching the rest. In 3.40, T17's tool re-sorted lines in that header and broke all 218 builds until it was fixed.
- **Against:** a few comment lines in those headers.

I think both are worth having. If you disagree with either one, I can remove it.

**So this doesn't happen again,** I've added a line to the card: every proposed rule gets this kind of plain explanation, covering what it requires, the incident behind it, and the case for and against, before you're asked to approve.

**One last open question.** Should the story and retrospective docs keep updating once per phase, as they do now, rather than every session as the old memory said? If yes, I'll note it on the card.

I've released the talk hold.

- The used/unused test is static. It counts a call in the third operand of `?:` as discarded, counts calls inside comma expressions as used, and does not see calls hidden in macros.

The def head is the source of truth for the spelling, because argcheck's def_ret is normalized.

## 183401-061r-claude-answer

**What a "site" is.** A site is one line of source that declares a function, in one file. The project keeps each matched function in its own small source file, across 218 binaries. That's tens of thousands of files, and each one carries its own copied declarations for every function it calls, for example `extern void func_8016130C();`. A "return-type lie" is a declaration line whose return type disagrees with the function's real definition. In that example, the function actually returns `s32`, and 1,213 files said `void`. T3 counted 273 functions declared wrongly somewhere, across 100,266 such lines.

**How 75k went away.** Nothing was deleted. A script rewrote one word on each lying line, in place: the declared return type became the one the definition uses (`void` became `s32`). This first batch fixed 182 functions on 75,801 lines in 3,927 files. These were the "safe" cases, where the return type shouldn't change the compiled bytes. Then the full rebuild checked that all 218 binaries were still byte-identical, and the batch was only kept once that passed.

The rebuild caught one function that wasn't actually safe. With `func_80139BE0` declared as returning `s32`, the compiler arranges registers differently, even at calls that throw the result away, so the bytes moved in 129 binaries. That one function and one wrongly detected function were left out. The rebuild then passed 218 of 218. What's left is 92 functions on 24,465 lines. T4.c2 is doing those now, checking every object's bytes one by one.

**Is this post-100% tech debt that day 1 would have avoided?** Mostly yes. The lies exist because every file got its own copy of declarations. Each copy was guessed when its function was matched, and nothing compared the copies to the real definitions. With one shared header declaring each function once, and every file including it, the compiler itself would have rejected most of these mismatches. One caveat makes it "mostly": `func_80139BE0` shows that some wrong-looking declarations were holding bytes in place. Even on day 1 those would have needed a cast at the call, so a shared header alone wouldn't have made everything clean.

**Is it being documented?** Partly.
- **Story and retrospective:** booked. T11 writes story §10 and retrospective §7, including the "sooner" question, which is where this lesson belongs. T9 adds the cookbook entries and a wiki page, "The type layer".
- **The graph: not covered.** The readability series behind the README graphs charts lying declarations by parameter count, but it has no column for return-type lies. So the 100,266 to 24,465 drop wouldn't show.
- **The day-1 guide (`docs/how-to-ai-decomp/`): not explicitly booked.** It already names a "canonical-signature layer that all files declare against", but only as a repair step (`10-integration-and-propagation.md:16`). It doesn't say to start with one shared header that the compiler checks, or that changing a declaration from `void` to `s32` can move bytes.

**My recommendation.** Add both to this phase's existing docs tasks:
- a return-lie column in the readability series, so the graph shows the drop;
- a day-1 lesson in the guide.

Neither changes the milestone, and both land in tasks that haven't started (T9 to T11), so nothing running is affected. The picker is open. I've released the talk hold, so T5 starts when T4 finishes.

PA3 is updated from 3.32.9 to 3.32.10. It's a hotfix with one visible change and three fixes for issues reported on GitHub.

- **Proposed rules get explained when you approve a plan.** Each rule comes with a short plain-English card before its question. The card says why the rule is proposed, what went wrong last phase, what it will fix and what it costs. Tool candidates get the same card. This is what you asked for after T2 and T3, now built into the plan view.
- **Reopened tasks no longer block the tasks after them.** When a task is reopened and the new version finishes, the tasks waiting on the old one now start. Before, they stayed blocked until the old versions were marked done by hand.
- **No more runaway copies of the usage-summary rebuild.** Only one rebuild runs at a time now. Before, a long rebuild could let more copies start, and they piled up at full CPU.
- **No more double answers.** When I answered quickly, PA3 could sometimes think the answer was lost and have a fresh Claude answer the same message again, occasionally with a second picker.

Project Architect 3.32.10, a hotfix (Rules explained before you choose, and three fixes from GitHub), is installed.

The end of the phase will have the context it needs. T4 doesn't need to write story or retrospective prose itself; its job is to leave good raw material, and it did. I checked its summary.

**How the context survives.** Every task writes three things while its work is still fresh:
- **A summary** (`phase-ends/current/tasks/T4.md`): what was done, the numbers before and after, the decisions and the findings.
- **A full log** for each coder run: the timeline, the commands, and what broke and why.
- **Cookbook entries** for anything other projects could use. T4 banked two. C0547 is the lesson that a `void` to `s32` change can move bytes even when the result is thrown away. C0548 is the order T4 tried fixes in for each function: first fix the declarations, then the definition, and otherwise record an exception.

T9 and T11, the docs tasks, are briefed to build the wiki, story and retrospective from those summaries. They don't rely on anyone remembering. This is the same reasoning as the once-per-phase story rule you approved: writing prose mid-phase mostly means rewriting it later.

**T4's summary has what the story will want:**
- 254 of the 273 functions are fixed.
- The other 19 are recorded with the exact instruction that moves. Each is a width or sign mismatch, such as `u8` against `int` or `short` against `int`, where changing either side changes the compiled code.
- One find is a nice story beat: 37 functions were defined `void`, but their callers read the return register. So T4 changed the definitions to `s32`, even though their bodies have no `return` statement. That's honest for the callers, but it's a readability item for later.

**The one real gap was the "why".** The answers you asked about came out of our conversation, not out of a task: what a site is, and the fact that a single shared header from day 1 would have prevented most of these. A docs task reading only task summaries could have missed that. Two things now cover it:
- **The filed records.** They hold that explanation, and any later Claude sees them.
- **The return-lie task we added.** It carries the day-1 lesson as a requirement it must finish.

**The graph is the one part that is timing-sensitive.** The readability series only gets a row at a snapshot, and the last one was at 3.40's close, so there's no row from mid-T4. That's fine, because T4's before and after counts are in its summary, and the new task backfills them as rows. If a task's numbers were never written down anywhere, they could only be rebuilt by checking out old commits. That's why each summary records them.

In short, tasks record facts as they go and the close turns them into the story. The only thing that needed adding was the reasoning from our conversation, and that's covered now. I've released the talk hold.

- duplicate-layout classes that are not listed as twins in `docs/struct-twins.md`;
- struct definitions outside the canonical headers (block-scope frames excluded);
- dead names;
- lying declarations, arity or return type, that are not ledgered in `config/lying_exceptions.tsv`.

`lever_census --check` now fails when a counted class A/B site's `// !FAKE:` marker names no instrument. Commit 33ea85f45e. All three verify commands pass with rc 0. The check reports "attributed 1,853 {P36 1817, P37 35, PA3 1}, 0 UNATTRIBUTED" on the same line as the unmarked count, and `--strict --residue` still exits 0.

**Instrument vocabulary.** It lives in the tool as `INSTRUMENT_FORMS`, three named forms with no catch-all, each tied to the phase that wrote it:
- **P36:** the S105 scratch script's regex, copied unchanged.
- **Legacy P37:** `P37 S+A t<n>_<batch>`, backed by the restruct batch commits ad290b568f (t4_S1), 7ffca89cab (t5_md_S1), ad9201b927 (t5_main_S1) and dfc798e28e (t17_ov_S1).
- **PA3:** `pass: 3.NN T<n>[.k]`, the form 3.39 T7.1 first wrote in `include/gte_inline.h`.

**Census and the one fix.** The census of today's markers found a single site with no instrument: a bare `// !FAKE: launder` that 3.40 T11.c106 wrote at `src/ov_SC06_025/ov_SC06_025_jr_8017EEC4.c:4964`. I rewrote its text from its residue row (`config/lever_residue.tsv:972`) to say `pass: 3.40 T11 crack G23; instrument: delever_search --try partial (29 tries)`.

**Proof.** On the real tree, putting the old marker back made `--check` exit 1 and name that site; with the fix it exits 0. The new selftest controls work as asked: a planted bare marker fails, and a P36-form and a 3.40 PA3-form marker pass. R22 gave 218 passed, 0 failed of 218. `make kit-corpus` and `make tools-health` are OK.

**Deviations.**
- I made the edit myself (about 40 lines) instead of briefing a coder.
- The "3.40 form" in the done-when is the PA3 `pass: 3.NN T<n>` form. Before this task, no 3.40 marker in the tree named an instrument.
- I fixed the marker text instead of accepting the residue row's instrument as a fallback, because a fallback would let future bare markers pass.

**Rule going forward.** Any new `// !FAKE:` marker must use the PA3 form; a new form is added to `INSTRUMENT_FORMS` with its phase, never widened. I wrote this into `docs/levers.md` §7 and marked it binding in the summary. The technique is banked as cookbook C0549.

This phase teaches Ghidra the struct types we designed in the C headers. Ghidra is the reverse-engineering tool that holds our view of the game's binaries. Once it has the types, when you or an agent look at a function in Ghidra, the data shows as named records with named fields, the same names the C uses, instead of bare offsets.

**Why it matters.** Over 3.38 to 3.40 we gave every struct one agreed definition, in `include/struct_types.h` and `src/shared/engine_types.h`. Ghidra never learned those types, so the two views of the game drift apart. The project's rule is that the headers are the single source of truth and Ghidra mirrors them. Ghidra is never edited by hand.

**What happens, in two steps:**
- **T7 (running now): build and prove it on a scratch copy.** A new tool, `tools/ghidra_types.py`, reads the two headers and writes the types out as Ghidra import rows. It uses gcc's own rules to place each field. Then a throwaway Ghidra project is rebuilt from those text files for each of the 6 programs, the main executable and the overlays included. The "proof" checks that the rebuilt database comes out right. It also has controls:
  - **A deliberate error.** One field is deliberately broken, and the proof must fail on it.
  - **A field-by-field match.** For at least 20 types, every field's position and size in Ghidra must equal what gcc says.

  A new check also fails whenever the headers change and the Ghidra rows weren't regenerated, and that check joins `make tools-health`. Your live Ghidra database isn't touched in this step.
- **T8 (next): apply it to your live database.** The same rows are imported into your real Ghidra project. Then you look at one struct, in Ghidra itself or through the MCP, and say it looks right. Nothing closes until you do.

**What it will need from you.** T7's expert noticed the MCP Ghidra is serving on port 8080 again; it most likely started with the new session. The proof rebuilds can't run beside it. So T7 will probably ask to stop it with the clean stop script, as T1 did, and I'll bring that question to you. Then at T8 the live import runs with it stopped, it's started again afterwards, and you run `/mcp` once to reconnect. I'll tell you exactly when.

**One finding so far.** T7's coder found three structs that hold tables of function pointers, and the shared layout parser misreads them. It's reporting the bug rather than patching it inside T7. I'll tell you how the expert handles it.

**Separately, from the last filing.** The 37 functions that became `s32` with no `return` statement are now in the inbox for 3.43, commit 119e85541e. I've released the talk hold.

Every canonical type in the two headers now reaches Ghidra from the repo text, and all 6 rebuild proofs print PROOF PASS with failed=0. I checked the 6 `.proof` markers, the import lines in the proof logs, both control logs and `ghidra_roster --check` myself. One gap: the full `make tools-health` was last green at c1 and was not re-run after c2 and c3, because it takes about 17 minutes and one call is capped at 285 s. The steps c2 and c3 could affect were re-run and are OK: the types check, the roster check and `make kit-corpus`.

**What was built**
- **Generator:** a new `tools/ghidra_types.py` writes 7,151 type rows (4,131 structs, 3,005 typedefs, 15 unions; the headers have no enums) into `config/ghidra/types/<prog>.jsonl`. Each program gets the types its translation units use, closed over the types they depend on.
  - The two prototypes have no translation units, so they take main's set.
  - The 6,014 types no program uses go to SLUS_007.26, so every type is in at least one program.
- **Where the rows live:** generated rows stay out of the hand-authored `config/ghidra/<prog>.jsonl` files. The rebuild merges both into export order, and the proof compares the delta against that merged file.
- **Staleness check:** `--check` takes about 6 s and is wired into tools-health. It fails on a stale or missing file, a type placed in no program, or a header member the parser dropped.
- **Ghidra scripts:** the import and export scripts gained bitfield support, and the import gained dependency ordering for typedefs and unions and a fix for two-dimensional arrays.
- **Function-pointer arrays:** three types made of arrays of function pointers came out as 1-byte shells. The generator now reads those members with `cdecl.py`, so the census's layout engine is unchanged.
- **Wiki:** the Ghidra rebuild page has a section on how types reach the database.

**Rows and proof wall times**

| Program | Rows | Proof wall time |
|---|---|---|
| SLUS_007.26 | 6,565 | 208 s |
| sep8_SLUS_007.26 | 394 | 206 s |
| aug31_USA_DEMO.EXE | 394 | 208 s |
| ov_SC01_077 | 593 | 172 s |
| ov_SC06_018 | 600 | 173 s |
| resident | 59 | 77 s |

**Controls**
- **Mutation:** changing one field of one type in a scratch copy of resident's rows (u32 to u16) gave PROOF FAIL. Restoring it gave PASS.
- **Layout against gcc:** the offsets and sizes in Ghidra's own export of SLUS_007.26 equal gcc's for all 3,772 types (5 unions and 7 bitfield structs included). The generated rows of all 6 files also equal gcc's: 5,221 types, 34,310 members.
- The proof only shows that Ghidra reproduces the rows exactly; the gcc comparison is what checks the layout.

**For Claude and T8:** the MCP is still stopped. T8 restarts it with `tools/ghidra_mcp_start.sh`, then the developer runs `/mcp`. Any future header edit now needs `ghidra_types.py --write`, or tools-health fails.

**Left uncommitted:** `make kit-corpus` keeps changing `decomp-architect/corpus/tools/PROJECT-ONLY/plan_edit.py`, which comes from someone else's uncommitted `plan_edit.py` edit, so it is not in any T7 commit.

Lessons are banked as cookbook C0550 and C0551. Commits: 711a7bb170, 7db6a2a877, ec3e3464b8, 20b66325f0, 150cad3292, 75b25f7e20.

- `coord` at +0x04, a 32-byte matrix (the frame's own position and rotation)

I compared it with the header, `include/struct_types.h:1890-1897`, and it matches field for field. The fields add up to the 80 bytes, and the layout matches the SDK's. If you want to see it with your own eyes, open the Data Type Manager in the Ghidra window and look under `/bfm`.
